newsitem.title: USA: NYCE cotton ends sharply up amid short covering.
newsitem.headline: NYCE cotton ends sharply up amid short covering.

text.p: NYCE cotton settled sharply up amid technically-driven short-covering that fueled prices to the highs just ahead of the close, floor sources said.
The December contract ended up 1.65 cents at 75.93 cents per lb, traded 77.00 to 75.40 cents. The rest of the board finished 1.36 to 1.10 cents firmer.

Commission house buying and speculative short-covering sent the most-active December contract through major sell stops at 76.25 cents, to a 13-week high of 77.00. The contract traded at 77.15 cents on March 17.
The trade remained an aggressive seller from 76.00 cents.
While prices are expected to climb higher on Wednesday, trade selling is likely to limit a rally.
"Given the magnitude of the close we could see some follow-through on Wednesday but all things considered, we may be a little bit extended," a dealer said.

On the fundamental side, expectations for a drop in the U.S. Department of Agriculture's planted area estimate provided further incentive to rally. Rain and wet weather throughout much of the cotton belt have led some growers to abandon cotton in favor of other crops.
The USDA will issue its final forecast on Monday. In March, the USDA said farmers would plant 14.485 million acres of cotton in the 1997/98 season.

Some trading sources said concern about flooding in Texas may have contributed to the rally. But Weather Services Corp forecast warm and dry weather in the cotton-growing areas over the next several days, which is expected to spur the growth of the West Texas crop.
Open interest in the July contract stood at 3,323 lots as of Monday, down 4,919 lots from the previous session.
Volume was estimated at a brisk 30,000 lots, compared with Monday's official 26,047 lots.
The U.S. Census Bureau today put mill consumption at a seasonally adjusted rate of 10.78 million bales in May, compared to a revised 10.91 million bales in April.
Demand-to-date was pegged at 10.80 million bales, slightly below the U.S. Department of Agriculture's estimate of 11.0 million bales for the 1996/97 season.
